Remember that the identity matrix [MATH: I_n] is an [MATH: n \times n] square matrix with [MATH: 1]'s on the diagonal, and where all other elements are [MATH: 0.] For example, the [MATH: 3 \times 3] identity matrix [MATH: I_3] is given below:

Content:
[MATH: [1|0|0; 0|1|0; 0|0|1]]

Content:
The identity matrix gets its name from the fact that whenever we multiply a matrix by the corresponding identity matrix, the matrix remains unchanged.

Content:
For example, let's consider the matrix

Content:
[MATH: [− 2|3|10; 6|− 2|2; 23|4|8]]

Content:
Multiplying the matrix [MATH: A] by the identity matrix [MATH: I_3,] we find that the result is just [MATH: A] itself:

Content:
[MATH: A ⋅ I_{3}|= [− 2|3|10; 6|− 2|2; 23|4|8][1|0|0; 0|1|0; 0|0|1]; = [(− 2) ⋅ 1 + 3 ⋅ 0 + 10 ⋅ 0|(− 2) ⋅ 0 + 3 ⋅ 1 + 10 ⋅ 0|(− 2) ⋅ 0 + 3 ⋅ 0 + 10 ⋅ 1; 6 ⋅ 1 + (− 2) ⋅ 0 + 2 ⋅ 0|6 ⋅ 0 + (− 2) ⋅ 1 + 2 ⋅ 0|6 ⋅ 0 + (− 2) ⋅ 0 + 2 ⋅ 1; 23 ⋅ 1 + 4 ⋅ 0 + 8 ⋅ 0|23 ⋅ 0 + 4 ⋅ 1 + 8 ⋅ 0|23 ⋅ 0 + 4 ⋅ 0 + 8 ⋅ 1]; = [− 2|3|10; 6|− 2|2; 23|4|8]; = A]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: A \cdot I_3 = A.] You can check that [MATH: I_3 \cdot A = A] using the same method.

Content:
This result holds in general:

Content:
> For any square [MATH: n \times n] matrix [MATH: A,] we have
> [MATH: A \cdot I_n = I_n \cdot A = A.]

Content:
In other words, the [MATH: n \times n] identity matrix [MATH: I_n] has a similar property to the number [MATH: 1,] namely that [MATH: a\cdot 1 = 1\cdot a = a] for any real number [MATH: a.]

Content:
We've been using the fact that [MATH: AI_n = I_n A = A] for any [MATH: n \times n] matrix [MATH: A.] But how do we know for sure?

Content:
Let's prove the case of [MATH: n=2.] That is, let's prove that [MATH: AI_2=I_2A = A,] where [MATH: A] is any [MATH: 2\times2] matrix.

Content:
Any general [MATH: 2 \times 2] matrix can be written as
[MATH: [a_{11}|a_{12}; a_{21}|a_{22}]]

Content:
Then, multiplying by [MATH: I_2,] we have

Content:
[MATH: AI_{2}|= [a_{11}|a_{12}; a_{21}|a_{22}][1|0; 0|1]; = [a_{11} ⋅ 1 + a_{12} ⋅ 0|a_{11} ⋅ 0 + a_{12} ⋅ 1; a_{21} ⋅ 1 + a_{22} ⋅ 0|a_{21} ⋅ 0 + a_{22} ⋅ 1]; = [a_{11}|a_{12}; a_{21}|a_{22}]; = A.]

Content:
Similarly,

Content:
[MATH: I_{2}A|= [1|0; 0|1][a_{11}|a_{12}; a_{21}|a_{22}]; = [a_{11}|a_{12}; a_{21}|a_{22}]; = A.]

Content:
The above proof shows that the property [MATH: A I_2 = I_2 A = A] holds for all [MATH: 2\times2] matrices [MATH: A.]

Content:
In general, to prove that the property [MATH: AI_n = I_n A = A] holds for all [MATH: n \times n] matrices [MATH: A,] we can use the same method.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Remember that the identity matrix [MATH: I_n] is an [MATH: n \times n] square matrix with [MATH: 1]'s on the diagonal, and where all other elements are [MATH: 0.] For example, the [MATH: 3 \times 3] identity matrix [MATH: I_3] is given below:

Content:
[MATH: [1|0|0; 0|1|0; 0|0|1]]

Content:
The identity matrix gets its name from the fact that whenever we multiply a matrix by the corresponding identity matrix, the matrix remains unchanged.

Content:
For example, let's consider the matrix

Content:
[MATH: [− 2|3|10; 6|− 2|2; 23|4|8]]

Content:
Multiplying the matrix [MATH: A] by the identity matrix [MATH: I_3,] we find that the result is just [MATH: A] itself:

Content:
[MATH: A ⋅ I_{3}|= [− 2|3|10; 6|− 2|2; 23|4|8][1|0|0; 0|1|0; 0|0|1]; = [(− 2) ⋅ 1 + 3 ⋅ 0 + 10 ⋅ 0|(− 2) ⋅ 0 + 3 ⋅ 1 + 10 ⋅ 0|(− 2) ⋅ 0 + 3 ⋅ 0 + 10 ⋅ 1; 6 ⋅ 1 + (− 2) ⋅ 0 + 2 ⋅ 0|6 ⋅ 0 + (− 2) ⋅ 1 + 2 ⋅ 0|6 ⋅ 0 + (− 2) ⋅ 0 + 2 ⋅ 1; 23 ⋅ 1 + 4 ⋅ 0 + 8 ⋅ 0|23 ⋅ 0 + 4 ⋅ 1 + 8 ⋅ 0|23 ⋅ 0 + 4 ⋅ 0 + 8 ⋅ 1]; = [− 2|3|10; 6|− 2|2; 23|4|8]; = A]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: A \cdot I_3 = A.] You can check that [MATH: I_3 \cdot A = A] using the same method.

Content:
This result holds in general:

Content:
> For any square [MATH: n \times n] matrix [MATH: A,] we have
> [MATH: A \cdot I_n = I_n \cdot A = A.]

Content:
In other words, the [MATH: n \times n] identity matrix [MATH: I_n] has a similar property to the number [MATH: 1,] namely that [MATH: a\cdot 1 = 1\cdot a = a] for any real number [MATH: a.]

Item 9 — Tutorial: Proving Properties Related to the Identity Matrix

Content:
We've been using the fact that [MATH: AI_n = I_n A = A] for any [MATH: n \times n] matrix [MATH: A.] But how do we know for sure?

Content:
Let's prove the case of [MATH: n=2.] That is, let's prove that [MATH: AI_2=I_2A = A,] where [MATH: A] is any [MATH: 2\times2] matrix.

Content:
Any general [MATH: 2 \times 2] matrix can be written as
[MATH: [a_{11}|a_{12}; a_{21}|a_{22}]]

Content:
Then, multiplying by [MATH: I_2,] we have

Content:
[MATH: AI_{2}|= [a_{11}|a_{12}; a_{21}|a_{22}][1|0; 0|1]; = [a_{11} ⋅ 1 + a_{12} ⋅ 0|a_{11} ⋅ 0 + a_{12} ⋅ 1; a_{21} ⋅ 1 + a_{22} ⋅ 0|a_{21} ⋅ 0 + a_{22} ⋅ 1]; = [a_{11}|a_{12}; a_{21}|a_{22}]; = A.]

Content:
Similarly,

Content:
[MATH: I_{2}A|= [1|0; 0|1][a_{11}|a_{12}; a_{21}|a_{22}]; = [a_{11}|a_{12}; a_{21}|a_{22}]; = A.]

Content:
The above proof shows that the property [MATH: A I_2 = I_2 A = A] holds for all [MATH: 2\times2] matrices [MATH: A.]

Content:
In general, to prove that the property [MATH: AI_n = I_n A = A] holds for all [MATH: n \times n] matrices [MATH: A,] we can use the same method.
